etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English coilen, from Old French coillir, cuillir (“to gather, pluck, pick, cull”) (modern French cueillir), from Latin colligō (“to gather together”), past participle collectus, from com- (“together”) + legō (“to gather”); compare legend. Doublet of cull.

definitions.definition: Something wound in the form of a helix or spiral.

quote.citation: 1819 June 23 – 1820 September 13, Geoffrey Crayon [pseudonym; Washington Irving], “(please specify the title)”, in The Sketch Book of Geoffrey Crayon, Gent., New York, N.Y.:  […]  C[ornelius] S. Van Winkle, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The wild grapevines that twisted their coils or tendrils from tree to tree.

definitions.definition: Any intrauterine device (abbreviation: IUD)—the first IUDs were coil-shaped.

quote.citation: 2020, Paul Mendez, Rainbow Milk, Dialogue Books (2021), page 293:
quote.text: ‘I’m gonna go on the pill and get fitted for a coil. I don’t wanna be pregnant. Ever. Again!’

definitions.definition: (electronics) A coil of electrically conductive wire through which electricity can flow.

quote.citation: a. 1722, Matthew Prior, “Human Life”, in H. Bunker Wright, Monroe K. Spears, editors, The Literary Works of Matthew Prior, Second edition, volume I, Oxford: Clarendon Press, published 1971, page 687:
quote.text: What trifling coil do we mortals keep;Wake, eat, and drink, evacuate, and sleep.

definitions.definition: To wind or reel e.g. a wire or rope into regular rings, often around a centerpiece.
To wind into loops (roughly) around a common center.
To build a pot (etc) with clay coils.
(obsolete, rare) To encircle and hold with, or as if with, coils.

quote.citation: a. 1757, Thomas Edwards, sonnet to Mr. Nathanael Mason
quote.text: Pleasure coil thee in her dangerous snare

definitions.definition: (now obsolete except in phrases) A noise, tumult, bustle, or turmoil.

quote.citation: a. 1738, Thomas Urquhart, Peter Anthony Motteux, and John Ozell (translators), François Rabelais, Gargantua and Pantagruel
quote.text: And when he saw that all the dogs were flocking about her, yarring at the retardment of their access to her, and every way keeping such a coil with her as they are wont to do about a proud or salt bitch, he forthwith departed  […]

quote.citation: c. 1588–1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Lamentable Tragedy of Titus Andronicus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, (please specify the scene number in lowercase Roman numerals)]:
quote.text: If the windes rage, doth not the Sea wax mad, / Threatning the welkin with his big-swolne face? / And wilt thou haue a reason for this coile?

quote.citation: 1624, John Smith, Generall Historie, Kupperman, published 1988, page 162:
quote.text: this great Savage desired also to see him. A great coyle there was to set him forward.

quote.citation: 1704, [Jonathan Swift], “Section IV”, in A Tale of a Tub. […], London:  […]  John Nutt, […], →OCLC, pages 99–100:
quote.text: [T]hey continued ſo extremely fond of Gold, that if Peter ſent them abroad, though it were only upon a Complement; they would Roar, and Spit, and Belch, and Piſs, and Fart, and Snivle out Fire, and keep a perpetual Coyl, till you flung them a Bit of Gold; [...]

quote.citation: 1897, Stanley John Weyman, “King Pepin and Sweet Clive”, in For the Cause:
quote.text: His liver demanded activity, namely, a quarrel, and what a coil this was!
